lit: two bundles for three mon (a tiny old coin): goods let go for almost nothing

use.how: Usually 二束三文で売る / 買い叩かれる, or 二束三文の〜. Said of goods or property that fetch a pitiful price, far below what they seem worth.

ctx.en: When I sold my old books, they fetched next to nothing.

ctx.s: 引[ひ]っ越[こ]しの前[まえ]に、家具[かぐ]を{二束三文[にそくさんもん]}で手放[てばな]した。
ctx.en: Before moving, I let my furniture go for a pittance.

ctx.s: 「ブランド物[もの]でも、傷[きず]があると{二束三文[にそくさんもん]}だよ。」
ctx.en: "Even designer goods are worth peanuts once they're scratched."

ctx.s: 「せっかく集[あつ]めたカードを{二束三文[にそくさんもん]}で売[う]るなんて、もったいないよ。」
ctx.en: "Selling the cards you worked so hard to collect for next to nothing? What a waste."

ctx.s: 倒産[とうさん]した会社[かいしゃ]の設備[せつび]は、{二束三文[にそくさんもん]}で買[か]い叩[たた]かれた。
ctx.en: The bankrupt company's equipment was bought up for a song.

bad.en: (meant: this restaurant is cheap and very tasty)
bad.why: It means worthless, sold off for nothing; it is never praise for good prices. For good value say yasukute oishii or o-tegoro.

bad.en: (meant: I've only got a little small change left in my wallet)

mean: getting rich quickly at one stroke

ctx.en: "Getting rich overnight isn't that easy, you know."

ctx.en: In the gold rush era, many people headed west hoping to make a fortune in one go.

ctx.s: 彼[かれ]は{一攫千金[いっかくせんきん]}の夢[ゆめ]を捨[す]てきれず、ギャンブルにのめり込[こ]んだ。
ctx.en: He couldn't give up his dream of a big windfall and sank deeper into gambling.

ctx.s: {一攫千金[いっかくせんきん]}を狙[ねら]うより、地道[じみち]に働[はたら]くほうが確実[かくじつ]だ。
ctx.en: Rather than chasing a quick fortune, steady work is the surer path.

bad.en: (meant: he is a rich man)

mean: so tense that a clash could erupt at any moment
lit: one touch, and it goes off at once

use.how: 一触即発の状態 / 雰囲気 / 危機, or as a predicate: 一触即発だ. Said of people, groups or countries locked in a standoff that has not exploded yet.

near.diff: 危機一髪 is a narrow escape from a danger that just happened; 一触即発 is a tense standoff before any clash has happened.

ctx.en: The confrontation between the two countries has deepened, and the danger of open conflict persists.

bad.en: (meant: the bookcase fell over in the earthquake and I only just escaped)

bad.en: (meant: he flew into a rage instantly)

lit: the road ahead holds many troubles

Its opposite: 前途洋々 says the future looks bright; 前途多難 says it looks hard.

ctx.s: 「英語[えいご]もできないのに留学[りゅうがく]？{前途多難[ぜんとたなん]}だけど、応援[おうえん]するよ。」

ctx.en: The new manager's first match ended in a heavy defeat, a troubled start to the new era.

bad.en: (meant: yesterday's exam was really hard)

bad.en: (meant: I got into university and a bright future awaits)
bad.why: Tanan means many hardships, so this is the opposite of congratulations. A bright future is zento yōyō.

mean: having a bright and promising future
lit: the road ahead stretches out wide, like a vast open sea

near.diff: 順風満帆 says things are going smoothly now; 前途洋々 says the future looks bright, often before much has happened.

ctx.en: "You're talented and still young. Your future is wide open."

ctx.s: 「{前途洋々[ぜんとようよう]}な若[わか]いお二人[ふたり]に、乾杯[かんぱい]！」

ctx.s: 卒業式[そつぎょうしき]で校長[こうちょう]は、{前途洋々[ぜんとようよう]}の卒業生[そつぎょうせい]たちにエールを送[おく]った。

ctx.s: 新人賞[しんじんしょう]を取[と]った彼女[かのじょ]の作家人生[さっかじんせい]は、{前途洋々[ぜんとようよう]}に見[み]えた。

ctx.s: 大[おお]きな契約[けいやく]も決[き]まり、できたばかりの会社[かいしゃ]は{前途洋々[ぜんとようよう]}だ。
ctx.en: With a big contract signed, the newly founded company has a bright future.

bad.why: It is about the future of a person or venture, not how a past event went. Say junchō de tanoshikatta.

bad.en: (meant: I wish your child a bright future)

mean: so suspicious that everything seems a threat
lit: a doubting heart sees demons in the dark

story.text: A man lost his axe and suspected his neighbour's son. Watching the boy, he found that his walk, his face and his words all looked like a thief's. Later the man found the axe while digging. The next time he saw the boy, nothing about him looked like a thief at all. A later commentary summed the story up as 'a doubting heart gives rise to demons in the dark', and the phrase comes from that.
story.source: 『列子』説符篇 (the lost axe) and a later commentary on it

use.how: Mostly 疑心暗鬼になる / 疑心暗鬼に陥る, or 疑心暗鬼が広がる. Said of people or groups who, after one doubt, start suspecting everyone and everything.

near.diff: 半信半疑 is half believing one claim; 疑心暗鬼 is suspicion spreading until innocent things look sinister.

ctx.s: 一度[いちど]だまされてから、{疑心暗鬼[ぎしんあんき]}になっている。
ctx.en: Ever since I was tricked once, I've been suspicious of everything.

ctx.en: "I feel like everyone's talking behind my back." "You're just being paranoid."

ctx.en: Just because my partner is a little late home, I start imagining the worst.

ctx.en: Distrust spread through the company, and no one said what they really thought anymore.

bad.s: このニュースが本当[ほんとう]かどうか、{疑心暗鬼[ぎしんあんき]}だ。
bad.en: (meant: I'm not sure whether this news is true)
bad.why: For doubting a single claim, say hanshin hangi. Gishin anki is suspicion grown so large that everything looks like a threat.

bad.en: (meant: I suspected the shop assistant and called the police)
bad.why: It is not a suru verb and takes no object; you gishin anki ni naru. To suspect a person, say ten'in o utagatte.

mean: giving up on oneself in despair
lit: doing violence to oneself and throwing oneself away

story.text: Mencius said that there is no talking with those who do violence to themselves, and no achieving anything with those who throw themselves away. To speak against propriety and righteousness is to do violence to yourself; to say 'I cannot live by benevolence and follow righteousness' is to throw yourself away. The two terms of that saying, jibō and jiki, were joined into this phrase.

use.how: 自暴自棄になる / 自暴自棄な生活, 自暴自棄にならないで. Said of someone who, after a failure or loss, stops caring what becomes of them.

near.diff: 意気消沈 is being downcast; 自暴自棄 goes further: giving up on yourself and acting recklessly against your own good.

bad.en: (meant: the trip was rained off and the children were disappointed)

lit: one's spirits fade away and sink

lit: waves ten thousand jō high (a jō is about three metres): a sea of huge, surging waves

near.diff: 紆余曲折 is the winding course a plan or process takes to an outcome; 波乱万丈 is a dramatic life or story.

ctx.en: "So that actor had a really eventful life, huh."

ctx.s: この映画[えいが]は、ある冒険家[ぼうけんか]の{波乱万丈[はらんばんじょう]}の生涯[しょうがい]を描[えが]いている。

ctx.s: 「私[わたし]の人生[じんせい]なんて、{波乱万丈[はらんばんじょう]}とはほど遠[とお]いよ。」

ctx.s: 自伝[じでん]には、戦後[せんご]を生[い]き抜[ぬ]いた{波乱万丈[はらんばんじょう]}の半生[はんせい]がつづられている。

mean: many twists and turns before reaching an outcome
lit: meandering and bending, like a road that keeps winding

use.how: Mostly 紆余曲折を経て + outcome, 紆余曲折の末, or 紆余曲折があった. Said of plans, negotiations, relationships or careers that reached a result by a complicated route.

near.diff: 試行錯誤 is deliberately trying methods until one works; 紆余曲折 is the complicated course events took on their own.
波乱万丈 is a dramatic life or story; 紆余曲折 stresses the winding path to one particular outcome.

cue: The station redevelopment was proposed, cancelled, redesigned twice and held up by lawsuits; ten years later it finally opened.

ctx.s: {紆余曲折[うよきょくせつ]}を経[へ]て、二人[ふたり]は結婚[けっこん]した。
ctx.en: After many twists and turns, the two of them got married.

ctx.s: 「この企画[きかく]が通[とお]るまで、いろいろ{紆余曲折[うよきょくせつ]}があったんですよ。」
ctx.en: "There were all sorts of ups and downs before this proposal got approved."

ctx.s: 新駅[しんえき]の建設[けんせつ]は、{紆余曲折[うよきょくせつ]}の末[すえ]ようやく実現[じつげん]した。
ctx.en: After a long and winding process, the new station was finally built.

ctx.s: {紆余曲折[うよきょくせつ]}はあったが、交渉[こうしょう]は最終的[さいしゅうてき]にまとまった。
ctx.en: There were complications, but the negotiations were concluded in the end.

ctx.s: 彼女[かのじょ]が教師[きょうし]になるまでには、多[おお]くの{紆余曲折[うよきょくせつ]}があった。
ctx.en: She went through many twists and turns before she became a teacher.

ctx.s: 様々[さまざま]な{紆余曲折[うよきょくせつ]}を乗[の]り越[こ]え、チームは初優勝[はつゆうしょう]を果[は]たした。
ctx.en: Having come through all kinds of twists and turns, the team won its first championship.

bad.s: 彼[かれ]は{紆余曲折[うよきょくせつ]}な性格[せいかく]で、付[つ]き合[あ]いにくい。
bad.en: (meant: he has a twisted personality and is hard to get along with)
bad.why: It describes the course events take, not a person's character. For a twisted, difficult person say hinekureta seikaku.

bad.s: 試験[しけん]に向[む]けて、{紆余曲折[うよきょくせつ]}して勉強法[べんきょうほう]を探[さが]した。
bad.en: (meant: I tried various study methods by trial and error before the exam)
bad.why: For deliberately trying methods until one works, say shikō sakugo shite. Uyo kyokusetsu is the winding course events took.
